text: Design & transition's purpose is to ensure products and services continually meet stakeholder expectations for quality, cost, and time to market, and that new or changed services move smoothly from development into live operation. Two concerns, one activity, on purpose.

A well-designed service that fails during rollout delivers no value. A smooth rollout of a poorly designed service just delivers the wrong thing faster. ITIL 4 treats design and transition as inseparable for exactly that reason — this lesson covers both halves together.

The design half turns requirements into a specification: what the service does, how it's built, what it costs, and how fast it can realistically ship. Quality, cost, and time-to-market are usually in tension, and this is where that trade-off gets made deliberately, not discovered by accident after launch.

The transition half is the handoff. Service design shapes the specification. Change enablement — its own practice, covered fully in Chapter 4 — assesses and authorizes the change going live. Release management controls when and how it reaches users. Service validation and testing confirms the result actually meets requirements before anyone depends on it.

Design & transition doesn't originate work on its own. It receives direction from Plan and needs from Engage, then produces a specified, tested, ready-to-operate result that becomes input to Obtain/build, and eventually to Deliver & support.

A weak transition step doesn't show up as a design defect. It shows up weeks later as incidents, repeat problems, or failed changes — the exact practices Chapter 4 covers. A lot of what looks like an incident management failure actually traces back to a transition that was rushed or skipped.
Design & transition turns a plan into something ready for real use. Next: Obtain/build and Deliver & support — getting the components, then actually running the thing day to day.
